title: L4 vs L7 Load Balancing
description: Understand the difference between TCP-level and HTTP-level load balancing, TLS termination, and content-based routing decisions.

segments.text: You've learned the algorithms. Now let's talk about where in the network stack your load balancer operates. This choice fundamentally changes what it can see, what it can do, and how fast it can do it.

Quick refresher. The OSI model has seven layers. Layer 4 is the transport layer, where TCP and UDP live. Layer 7 is the application layer, where HTTP, gRPC, and WebSocket live. Load balancers operate at one of these two layers.

An L4 load balancer works at the TCP level. It sees IP addresses and port numbers, but it never reads the actual HTTP request. It forwards raw TCP connections to backend servers. Think of it as a postal worker who routes by zip code without reading the letter.
Because L4 doesn't parse HTTP, it's incredibly fast. It can handle millions of connections per second with minimal latency. HAProxy in TCP mode and AWS Network Load Balancer are classic examples.
An L7 load balancer opens the HTTP envelope. It reads headers, URLs, cookies, and even request bodies. This means it can make intelligent routing decisions based on the actual content of the request.

With L7, you can route /api requests to your backend services, /images to a CDN origin, and /admin to a special secured cluster. You can even route based on headers, like sending mobile users to optimized servers.
segments.thought_prompt: What other HTTP fields could you use for smart routing decisions?

segments.text: Here's a critical capability of L7 load balancers: TLS termination. The load balancer decrypts HTTPS traffic, inspects it, makes routing decisions, then optionally re-encrypts before forwarding. This offloads expensive crypto work from your application servers.

But TLS termination means the load balancer sees plaintext traffic. In high-security environments, you might need end-to-end encryption, which pushes you back toward L4. Security versus flexibility, always a trade-off.

Use L4 when you need raw speed, when your protocol isn't HTTP, or when you're handling TCP-based services like databases and message brokers. L4 is also ideal when you don't need to inspect request content.
Use L7 when you need path-based routing, A/B testing, canary deployments, rate limiting per endpoint, or authentication at the edge. Most modern web applications benefit from L7 load balancing.
segments.thought_prompt: Could you combine L4 and L7 load balancers in the same architecture? How?

segments.text: In practice, many architectures use both. An L4 load balancer at the edge distributes traffic across multiple L7 load balancers, which then make content-aware routing decisions. This gives you the throughput of L4 with the intelligence of L7.

Remember: L4 is fast but blind, L7 is smart but slower. The right choice depends on what you need to see and how fast you need to see it. That's the engineering trade-off you'll face in every load balancing design.
